name: Belgian Dutch (Flemish)
notes: Flemish / Belgian Dutch (Vlaams). Alveolar /r/ [r] in most varieties (vs. NL uvular [ʀ]). /ɣ/ (voiced velar fricative) more robust than in NL Dutch. Considered more conservative than Netherlands Dutch in some features. Strong dialect continuum from West-Flemish to Limburgish. Source: König & van der Auwera (1994). ⟨w⟩ (Verhoeven 2005, JIPA 35(2)): "[w] has a labial-velar articulation rather than labiodental in many accents of Netherlandic Dutch" (p. 245), with "w waːʀ̥ waar 'true'" in the word list (p. 244). So ⟨w⟩ is [w], against the [ʋ] of nl-NL, and the consonant that ⟨ieuw eeuw uw⟩ give before a vowel is [w] too: leeuwen [leːwən], nieuwe [niwə], duwen [dywən]. Paardekooper (1987, ABN-uitspraakgids, p. XVIII) notes the same bilabial w "in veel zuidelijke dialecten". ⟨g ch⟩ (Verhoeven 2005, p. 244): "Belgian Dutch has a voiced and voiceless velar fricative: these are absent in the Netherlands", with "x xɛil chijl" and "ɣ ɣɛil geil" in the word list. So nl-BE restates the velar values of ⟨g ch sch berg brecht⟩ against the uvular [χ] of nl-NL. ⟨ee eu oo⟩ and the open-syllable ⟨e o⟩ (Verhoeven 2005, pp. 245-246): "In Belgian Dutch, however, they are always monophthongs". So nl-BE disables the six NL_MID_TENSE_* rules by id and keeps [eː øː oː] against the closing diphthongs [ei øy ou] of nl-NL.

allophone_rules.notes: Verhoeven (2005, JIPA 35(2), pp. 245-246): "The main difference between Belgian Dutch and Netherlandic Dutch has to do with the pronunciation of the half-close long vowels [eː], [øː] and [oː]. In the Netherlands, these are frequently diphthongized. In Belgian Dutch, however, they are always monophthongs." So nl-BE disables the inherited nl-NL rule and keeps the monophthong.
